newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Templeton seeks SEC ruling on S.Africa asset swaps.
newsitem.headline: Templeton seeks SEC ruling on S.Africa asset swaps.

text.p: Templeton Asset Management SA, a subsidiary of the U.S.-based fund manager, said on Friday it was seeking a Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) ruling on whether certain South African asset swaps might contravene U.S. law.
Managing director John Phillips said the company, which has $800 million under management, had not engaged in any swaps pending clarification from the U.S. watchdog.
Templeton is concerned that so-called "quid pro quo" swaps might be illegal under U.S. law since companies could end up earning two fees, creating a potential clash with their fiduciary duties.
The group petitioned the SEC for an exemptive order giving a green light to South African asset swaps three months ago and hopes to receive a ruling soon, Phillips told Reuters.
"There is a possible conflict of interests on which we are asking the SEC to rule," he said.

The legal uncertainty arises because of the 1940 U.S. Investment Company Act, which prohibits an investment company from receiving any additional fees in addition to management fees as a result of a trasaction.

Such double fees can arise with South African asset swaps if the same investment company that carried out the swap is then hired to manage the foreign credit issued to the local company by the Reserve Bank, he said.
However, not all South African swaps work on this quid pro quo basis.

In some cases, two parties simply swap assets directly -- for example, certain South African shares in exchange for international shares. In other cases, a third party may be appointed as manager, thereby avoiding any potential conflict.

The Reserve Bank introduced the concept of asset swaps in July 1995, whereby local institutions could trade assets held domestically for those of a foreign partner. The swaps can include both equities and bonds.
A total of nearly 15 billion rand in asset swaps have been authorised since last July.
Reserve Bank officials were not immediately available to comment.
